source_question.stem: In combinatorial graph theory, Hall's Marriage Theorem states that a finite bipartite graph $G = (X, Y, E)$ has a complete matching saturating $X$ if and only if $|N(S)| \ge |S|$ for all $S \subseteq X$, where $N(S)$ denotes the neighborhood of $S$ in $Y$. Which of the following statements rigorously explains the structural obstruction mechanism that causes a matching saturating $X$ to fail when Hall's condition is violated?

options.label: A
options.text: If Hall's condition fails, there exists a certifying witness subset $S^* \subseteq X$ with $|N(S^*)| < |S^*|$; because all edges incident to $S^*$ must terminate in $N(S^*)$, the Pigeonhole Principle dictates that any matching can cover at most $|N(S^*)|$ vertices of $S^*$, leaving at least $|S^*| - |N(S^*)| \ge 1$ vertices in $S^*$ unmatched.

options.label: B
options.text: If Hall's condition fails, the graph contains an odd-length cycle, which by König's theorem prevents the existence of any independent edge set.

options.label: C
options.text: When $|N(S)| < |S|$, the degree sum of vertices in $S$ exceeds the degree sum of vertices in $N(S)$, violating the Handshaking Lemma.

options.label: D
options.text: The failure of Hall's condition implies that the chromatic number of $G$ must be strictly greater than $2$, so no bipartition can support independent edges.

answer.value: If Hall's condition fails, there exists a certifying witness subset S* with |N(S*)| < |S*|; all edges from S* terminate in N(S*), so by the Pigeonhole Principle at most |N(S*)| vertices of S* can be matched

hint_ladder.hint1_conceptual_nudge: Recall that in any matching $M$, distinct vertices in $X$ must be matched to distinct vertices in $Y$. If we restrict our attention to a subset $S \subseteq X$, where must their matched partners in $Y$ lie?
hint_ladder.hint2_tactical_step: Because the matched targets of any choice $S$ are restricted to its adjacent set $N(S)$, what is the upper capacity bound on how many independent edges can connect $S$ to $Y$ when $|N(S)| < |S|$?

distractor_rationales.opt-B: Bipartite graphs by definition contain no odd cycles; Hall's condition applies specifically to bipartite graphs.
distractor_rationales.opt-C: Sum of degrees in a subset does not equal the vertex count; $|N(S)| < |S|$ does not contradict the Handshaking Lemma.
distractor_rationales.opt-D: All bipartite graphs are 2-colorable; the chromatic number remains 2 regardless of matching existence.

core1a.title: Structural Barriers and Invariants in Bipartite Matchings
core1a.concept: In a bipartite graph $G = (X, Y, E)$, a matching is an independent set of edges. Hall's condition requires that every subset of $X$ has at least as many neighbors in $Y$ as its cardinality. The necessity of this condition arises from capacity constraints on the neighborhood sets.
core1a.boundary_conditions: If $X = \emptyset$, the condition holds vacuously. If $|X| > |Y|$, taking $S = X$ immediately gives $|N(X)| \le |Y| < |X|$.

core1b.prediction_prompt: In a bipartite graph $G = (X, Y, E)$, if $S \subseteq X$, can any vertex in $S$ have an edge to a vertex outside $N(S)$?
scaffold_steps: Observe all edges incident to S have endpoints in N(S)
Conclude matched edges from S are bounded by |N(S)|

html_representation:
In combinatorial graph theory, Hall's Marriage Theorem states that a finite bipartite graph $G = (X, Y, E)$ has a complete matching saturating $X$ if and only if $|N(S)| \ge |S|$ for all $S \subseteq X$, where $N(S)$ denotes the neighborhood of $S$ in $Y$. Which of the following statements rigorously explains the structural obstruction mechanism that causes a matching saturating $X$ to fail when Hall's condition is violated?

Recall that in any matching $M$, distinct vertices in $X$ must be matched to distinct vertices in $Y$. If we restrict our attention to a subset $S \subseteq X$, where must their matched partners in $Y$ lie?

Because the matched targets of any choice $S$ are restricted to its adjacent set $N(S)$, what is the upper capacity bound on how many independent edges can connect $S$ to $Y$ when $|N(S)| < |S|$?

Review Hall Marriage Obstruction
Show Complete Olympiad Derivation

1. Formal definition of complete matching:

A matching saturating $X$ is a subset of edges $M \subseteq E$ such that every vertex $x \in X$ is incident to exactly one edge in $M$, and no two edges in $M$ share a common vertex.

2. Restriction of matching edges to a subset $S$:

Let $S \subseteq X$ be an arbitrary non-empty subset. For any matching $M$, let $M_S = \{e \in M : e \text{ is incident to a vertex in } S\}$.

By the bipartite definition, every edge incident to $S$ has its other endpoint in $Y$. Specifically, the other endpoint must belong to the open neighborhood $N(S) = \{y \in Y : \exists s \in S, (s, y) \in E\}$.

3. Upper bound via Pigeonhole Principle:

Because edges in $M$ are mutually disjoint, each edge in $M_S$ must terminate at a distinct vertex of $N(S)$.

Therefore, the total number of matched edges incident to $S$ cannot exceed the cardinality of available targets in $Y$:

$|M_S| \le |N(S)|$.

4. Structural obstruction when Hall's condition is violated:

If Hall's condition fails, there exists a certifying witness subset $S^* \subseteq X$ such that:

$|N(S^*)| < |S^*|$.

Substituting this strict inequality into the capacity bound yields:

$|M_{S^*}| \le |N(S^*)| < |S^*|$.

Because each edge in $M_{S^*}$ covers exactly one vertex in $S^*$, the total number of vertices in $S^*$ covered by the matching $M$ is $|M_{S^*}| < |S^*|$.

5. Inescapable deficit:

This guarantees that at least $|S^*| - |N(S^*)| \ge 1$ vertices in $S^*$ must remain unmatched in any matching $M$.

No augmenting path can ever resolve this defect, because any augmenting path must alternate through $N(S^*)$, which cannot accommodate more than $|N(S^*)|$ disjoint connections.
